pages.text: A mirror of diameter D gathers light in proportion to D², so the faintest star it records - the limiting magnitude - rises by 5·log₁₀ D, and by 2.5·log₁₀ for every tenfold longer exposure. The air smears every star into a seeing disc; the mirror itself cannot do better than its diffraction limit, 1.22λ/D. A moonlit sky is brighter, and drowns the faintest stars.
$(thing)Set$(): Aperture D, Exposure t.$(br2)$(thing)Disturbance$(): Turbulence: the seeing varies by ±15%·d.

$(thing)Limits$(): The sky is too bright: a telescope works only at night; Something blocks the sky above the slit; Overcast: no stars tonight.$(br2)$(thing)Rate$(): Deeper than the target needs is faster; very long exposures are slower.

$(thing)Equations$()$(br)Seeing: θ_see ≈ 2.5″·e^(−(h − 64)/120)$(br)Diffraction limit: θ = 1.22λ/D$(br)Resolution: θ = √(θ_diff² + θ_see²)$(br)Sky brightness: μ_sky$(br)Limiting magnitude: m_lim ≈ m₀ + 5 log D + 1.25 log t + ½(μ − μ₀) − 2.5 log θ
